To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the model-based influences on human choices were significantly reduced when the model-based influences were not consistent with the model-free influences, and 2) these effects were associated with increased activity in the ventral striatum and decreased activity in the dorsal striatum.
(1) the striatum tracks prediction error in a model-based reinforcement learning task and (2) the striatum is sensitive to the structure of a model-based reinforcement.
(1) model-based influences on choices and (2) striatal prediction errors are both modulated by the model-based influences.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the human striatum in the context of decision making and learning.
the role that the brain plays in the generation of human choices and in the evaluation of the consequences of these choices.
the way humans make choices and the way they learn from their choices and their outcomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the striatal prediction errors are a function of both the reward and the model-based influences.
there are two types of prediction errors: the one is a model-free error, and the other is a model-based error.

the striatum does not encode prediction error per se, but instead, it encodes the difference between the expected value of the chosen action (the value of the action that was chosen, given the current context) and the actual outcome (the actual outcome that occurred, given the current action).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain is a predictive machine, which is continuously predicting the future based on past experiences.
model-based learning is not just an internal process that is independent of choice.
the model-based influence of the striatum is not only about prediction errors but is about the model-based influence on the choices.
